1.symbols: $i,j$: neuron indices among $N$ cells; $N$: cell count. $t$: time (s). $s_i(t)$: outgoing synaptic activation of cell $i$, dimensionless because one spike adds one unit. $N_i(t)$: number of cell $i$'s spikes by time $t$; $dN_i$: new spikes in $dt$. $\tau$: synaptic decay time (s). $W_{ij}$: fixed connection from sender $j$ to receiver $i$, in input units per activation unit. $g_i,b_i$: total input and constant bias, in the same input units. $r_i$: firing rate (spikes/s). $\phi$: transfer function from input to rate.
1.paper_location: Main, Materials and Methods, Neural Network, Eqs. 7-9, PDF p. 5 (Early Edition 5 of 6). The count-increment equation is the guide's equivalent form of the impulse-train Eq. 7.
1.status: Paper model; first formula is an exact count-process rewrite of paper Eq. 7, rather than its printed notation.

2.symbols: $i$: neuron index. $K_i$: cell $i$'s spike count in the observation interval, dimensionless; this is not the matrix $K$ in M3. $\theta$: fixed represented value, in coordinate units such as radians. $h$: observation duration (s). $\bar r_i(\theta)$: steady firing rate at that value (spikes/s); bar means a steady value. $\lambda_i=h\bar r_i$: expected spike count, dimensionless. Poisson names the count distribution.
2.paper_location: SI, IV. Internal Fisher Information, Eq. S43, PDF p. 9, displays the joint product-Poisson likelihood with observation duration $\delta t$ and counts $n_i$. Main Eq. 9, PDF p. 5, states the Poisson spike model. Equal mean and variance and the rare-event derivation are worked out in the guide, not separately displayed source results.
2.guide_location: [Chapter 1, §1.4, A variable spike count at a fixed rate](../chapters/ch-foundations.html#sec-foundations-poisson).
2.status: Paper count model with guide aliases $K_i,h,\lambda_i$; the count moments and elementary derivation are exact properties of that model when the state is held fixed.

3.symbols: $i$: cell index; $N$: number of cells. $\theta$: represented coordinate (for example radians). $\bar{\mathbf s}(\theta)$ and $\delta\mathbf s$: steady activation and a small activation disturbance, both $N$-vectors of unit-spike activation. $\bar r_i$: steady rate (spikes/s). $K$: $N\times N$ linear response matrix (s$^{-1}$), distinct from spike count $K_i$. $\mathbf u=\partial\bar{\mathbf s}/\partial\theta$: tangent $N$-vector, activation per coordinate unit. $\mathbf v$: left zero-mode $N$-vector, coordinate units per activation; $v_i$ is its cell-$i$ entry. $\mathbf v^T\delta\mathbf s$: retained coordinate shift. $D(\theta)$: scalar diffusion coefficient, coordinate units squared/s; $2D$ is displacement variance per second.
3.paper_location: SI, II. The Coefficient of Diffusion: Eqs. S8-S9 define $K$, S11 gives $\mathbf u$, S12-S13 give the left-vector condition and normalization, and S14-S15 give projected variance and $2D$. All are on PDF p. 3. $K\mathbf u=0$ follows by differentiating the fixed-point family and is explained in the guide.
3.guide_location: [Chapter 3, §3.2, The network's return flow determines the lasting memory change](../chapters/ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization); [§3.3, Projecting spike fluctuations gives the diffusion coefficient](../chapters/ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion).
3.status: Paper leading weak-noise result. The guide supplies the explicit tangent differentiation and explains why the left vector gives the lasting change.

4.symbols: $i,j$: neuron indices among $N$ cells. $D$: scalar diffusion coefficient (coordinate units squared/s). $\theta$: represented coordinate. $\bar r_i$: steady rate (spikes/s); $\bar r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta$: tuning slope (rate per coordinate unit). $g_i$: steady total input in this formula; $g_i'=dg_i/d\theta$: input slope. $\tau$: synaptic decay time (s). $W$: $N\times N$ connection matrix (input units per activation unit); $W_{ij}=W_{ji}$ is pairwise symmetry. $\mathbf u=\partial\bar{\mathbf s}/\partial\theta$: tangent vector (activation per coordinate). $\mathbf v$: normalized left zero vector (coordinate per activation). Primes here mean first derivatives, not second derivatives.
4.paper_location: SI, II. The Coefficient of Diffusion, Eqs. S16-S18, PDF p. 4: S18 displays the squared input slope in the numerator and the full formula. Main Eq. 2, PDF p. 2, omits that square in the supplied Early Edition PDF. The guide links the 2017 author correction for main Eq. 2.
4.guide_location: [Chapter 3, §3.4, Symmetric weights express diffusion through tuning curves](../chapters/ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-symmetric).
4.status: Corrected source expression, directly supported by SI S18. It uses symmetric weights, the tuned continuous family and the same leading weak-noise assumptions.

5.symbols: $i=1,\ldots,N$: cell index; $N$: cell count. $\alpha,\beta=1,\ldots,m$: stored-coordinate indices, not thinning probabilities; $m$: number of coordinates. $\boldsymbol\theta$: $m$-vector of stored coordinates. $\bar r_i$: steady rate (spikes/s); $\partial_\alpha\bar r_i=\partial\bar r_i/\partial\theta_\alpha$: slope in coordinate $\alpha$. $\mathbf u^\beta$: $N$-vector tangent $\partial\bar{\mathbf s}/\partial\theta_\beta$ (activation per unit of coordinate $\beta$). $\mathbf v^\alpha$: matching left $N$-vector (units of coordinate $\alpha$ per activation). $\delta_{\alpha\beta}$: 1 for equal indices, otherwise 0. $D$: $m\times m$ diffusion matrix; $D_{\alpha\beta}$ has units coordinate-$\alpha$ times coordinate-$\beta$/s. $J$: invertible $m\times m$ information-rate matrix; $J_{\alpha\beta}$ has inverse coordinate-$\alpha$ times inverse coordinate-$\beta$/s. $\tau$: common decay time (s). $\succeq$ means the difference has a nonnegative quadratic form in every direction.
5.paper_location: SI: S21 defines $D$ on PDF p. 5; S22-S24 give tangents, normalization and the displayed diffusion tensor on p. 6. S44 displays the information matrix on p. 10. S52 displays the matrix bound on p. 11; S53-S56 prove it on p. 12. [Information matrix](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=10); [matrix bound](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=11); [proof](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=12).
5.guide_location: [Chapter 3, §3.3, Projecting spike fluctuations gives the diffusion coefficient](../chapters/ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion); [Chapter 5, §5.2, Spike information sets a lower bound on memory diffusion, matrix derivation](../chapters/ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-bound).
5.status: Paper diffusion and information matrices and paper matrix inequality; guide proof uses an equivalent nonnegative residual matrix. The ordinary inverse needs nonsingular $J$.

6.symbols: $t$: elapsed storage time (s). $\theta(t)$: current represented scalar value; $\Theta$: common initial value, in the same coordinate units. $p(\theta,t)$: probability density across trials, in inverse coordinate units. $D(\theta)$: local scalar diffusion coefficient (coordinate units squared/s); the later two formulas take it constant. $\mathbb E[D(\theta)]$: trial-averaged coefficient. MSD means mean squared displacement (coordinate units squared). For the circle example, $\theta$ is an angle in radians, reported error lies in $[-\pi,\pi)$ and $\pi^2/3$ is in rad$^2$.
6.paper_location: SI, III. Diffusive Dynamics Along the Attractor: S28-S30, PDF p. 7, give the density equation, point initial condition and Gaussian with variance $2Dt$. S31 (p. 7) and S32 (p. 8) give the wrapped density and angular-error moment. The limit $\pi^2/3$ and the moment-rate identity $d\operatorname{Var}/dt=2\mathbb E[D]$ are exact guide deductions under the displayed diffusion model and suitable boundary conditions, not separately displayed source formulas.
6.guide_location: [Chapter 4, §4.1, Long delay errors depend on boundaries and local diffusion](../chapters/ch-memory-long-delays.html#sec-memory-long-time).
6.status: Paper diffusion equation and constant-$D$ line solution; guide derives the circle's uniform-error limit and the general variance-rate identity. These assume zero systematic drift and the appropriate boundary rules.

7.symbols: $i$: neuron index. $\theta$: represented scalar value (for example radians). $\bar r_i(\theta)$: steady firing rate (spikes/s); $\bar r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta$: rate slope per coordinate unit. $h$: short observation duration (s), with the state effectively fixed. $J(\theta)$: scalar Fisher information per second, in inverse coordinate units squared/s. $I_h=hJ$: information in that observation, in inverse coordinate units squared. $\hat\theta$: estimate formed from the counts; its variance is in coordinate units squared.
7.paper_location: Main Eq. 3, PDF p. 2, displays $J$. SI IV, S42-S43, PDF p. 9, defines information per short interval and gives the Poisson likelihood; its continuation on p. 10 refers to the standard population-code derivation. Main, Information-Diffusion Inequality, PDF p. 3, invokes the Cramer Rao error bound in prose. The explicit score proof and $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)\ge1/(hJ)$ display are guide derivations of that standard bound, not separately numbered equations in this paper.
7.guide_location: [Chapter 5, §5.1, Rate slopes and spike variability determine local information](../chapters/ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-fi).
7.status: Paper information-rate formula plus a guide derivation of its count-information relation and the regular locally unbiased estimation bound.

8.symbols: $D$: scalar diffusion coefficient (coordinate units squared/s). $J$: scalar information rate about the same coordinate (inverse coordinate units squared/s). $\tau$: common synaptic decay time (s). $i$: neuron index. $\bar r_i$: steady rate (spikes/s); $\bar r_i'$: derivative of rate with respect to the represented coordinate. $v_i$: retained coordinate shift per unit activation change in cell $i$. Thus $2DJ\tau^2$ is dimensionless.
8.paper_location: Main, Information-Diffusion Inequality, Eq. 4, PDF p. 3, displays $D\ge J^{-1}/(2\tau^2)$. SI V, S45-S49, PDF pp. 10-11, proves it; S49 on p. 11 displays $2DJ\ge\tau^{-2}$. The row's Cauchy Schwarz proof is the guide's shorter equivalent proof.
8.guide_location: [Chapter 5, §5.2, Spike information sets a lower bound on memory diffusion](../chapters/ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-bound).
8.status: Paper inequality for the tuned weak-noise model; the dimensionless form is exact algebra. Symmetric connections are not required.

9.symbols: $i$: neuron index; $N$: neuron count. $\theta$: represented coordinate. $\bar r_i$: steady rate (spikes/s); $\bar r_i'$: its slope per coordinate unit. $v_i$: retained coordinate shift per activation unit. $J$: scalar information rate (inverse coordinate units squared/s). $\tau$: common decay time (s). $g$: total input, in model input units. $\phi(g)$: firing-rate response (spikes/s); $\phi'$ is its input derivative. $A>0$: rate scale (spikes/s). $k>0$: input sensitivity (inverse input units), so $kg$ is dimensionless. $W$: $N\times N$ connection matrix (input units per activation unit); $W=W^T$ means symmetric weights.
9.paper_location: SI V, Saturation of the inequality, following S49 through S51, PDF p. 11, gives the equality condition and exponential transfer class. Main, Saturation of the information-diffusion inequality, PDF p. 3, states exponential sufficiency. The explicitly normalized $v_i=\bar r_i'/(\tau J\bar r_i)$ is the guide's exact equality-condition reconstruction, not an equation printed in that form. The source's stronger exponential-necessity claim is qualified by the guide's linear counterexample.
9.guide_location: [Chapter 5, §5.2, Spike information sets a lower bound on memory diffusion, equality condition and linear counterexample](../chapters/ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-bound).
9.status: Paper sufficient exponential class; guide-derived explicit normalized equality condition and guide qualification of the source's necessity claim.

10.symbols: $N$: number of comparable neurons, a dimensionless count. $J$: scalar information rate (inverse coordinate units squared/s). $D$: scalar diffusion coefficient (coordinate units squared/s). $c>0$: dimensionless multiplier of every rate tuning curve and its slope; this scalar is unrelated to the preferred-value vector $\mathbf c$ in M11. $\tau$: synaptic decay time (s). Each proportionality describes a controlled change with the other properties specified in the derivation kept fixed.
10.paper_location: Main, Diffusive Drift due to Ongoing Neural Noise, paragraph following Eq. 2, PDF p. 2, states the network-size, firing-rate and decay-time comparisons. SI I, PDF pp. 1-2, gives population replication and $1/N$ weight scaling, including S6 for a ring. The explicit proportionality powers and $J\mapsto cJ$, $D\mapsto D/c$ are guide algebra from corrected Eq. 2 and Eq. 3 under the listed constraints, not a separately displayed source equation.
10.guide_location: [Chapter 5, §5.3, Improving persistence depends on what a comparison holds fixed](../chapters/ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-comparisons).
10.status: Guide-derived scaling relationships supporting paper comparisons. The rate-to-diffusion scaling needs equality in the bound or preserved tuning/input geometry; changing $\tau$ here holds rate tuning fixed by adjusting the circuit.

11.symbols: $d$: number of stored spatial coordinates, a positive integer. $\alpha$: one coordinate index. $\boldsymbol\theta$ and $\mathbf c$: $d$-vectors of represented position and a cell's preferred position, in coordinate units; $\mathbf c$ is not the scalar rate multiplier in M10. $w>0$: common tuning width (coordinate units). $a$: fixed peak firing rate (spikes/s). $f$: fixed dimensionless radial tuning shape, with dimensionless argument $(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w$. $\rho$: number of preferred positions per coordinate-volume, units coordinate$^{-d}$. $J,D$: $d\times d$ information-rate and diffusion matrices; $J_{\alpha\alpha}$ is inverse coordinate units squared/s, $D_{\alpha\alpha}$ is coordinate units squared/s.
11.paper_location: Main, discussion of internal information and tuning width, PDF p. 4, states that narrower curves help in 1D and broader curves in 3D and cites sensory coding work (ref. 31). The displayed $w^{d-2}$ and $w^{2-d}$ power laws and the integral derivation are guide reconstructions under fixed peak rate, uniform center density, radial shape and equality in the matrix bound. They are not formulas displayed in this paper.
11.guide_location: [Chapter 5, §5.3, Improving persistence depends on what a comparison holds fixed, tuning-width integral](../chapters/ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-comparisons).
11.status: Guide-derived scaling laws explaining a paper argument under explicit resource and symmetry assumptions; the diffusion power additionally assumes a circuit that attains the information bound.

12.symbols: $L$: duration of observation after the recall cue (s), called $\Delta T$ in the source; it is not the earlier storage delay $T$. $V_{\rm naive}(L)$: variance of error in estimating the cue-time state with equal observation weights (coordinate units squared). $L_{\rm naive}^*$: duration minimizing this variance (s). $D$: constant local diffusion coefficient (coordinate units squared/s). $J$: constant local information rate (inverse coordinate units squared/s). In $2D\min(t,s)$, $t,s$ are two elapsed observation times (s), and $s$ here is not synaptic activation. State-motion and observation noises are separate in this Gaussian readout model.
12.paper_location: SI VI, Naive estimator, S76-S79, PDF p. 15, gives the equal-weight estimator, Brownian time covariance and displayed variance. S80 on p. 15 gives the optimal duration; S81 on p. 16 gives its minimum variance. The double covariance integral in the guide exposes the cross-time terms absent from the printed S77 sum-of-squares line.
12.guide_location: [Chapter 6, §6.2, Equal weighting becomes harmful when observation lasts too long](../chapters/ch-memory-readout.html#sec-memory-naive).
12.status: Paper Gaussian-readout result; guide derives S79 explicitly through the covariance integral. This variance concerns reading the cue state, before adding storage error.

13.symbols: $L$: observation duration after the recall cue (s), source $\Delta T$; $L^*$: characteristic approach time (s), not a finite optimum. $D$: constant local scalar diffusion coefficient (coordinate units squared/s). $J$: constant scalar information rate (inverse coordinate units squared/s). $V_{\rm ideal}(L)$: ideal cue-state readout-error variance (coordinate units squared); $V_{\rm ideal}(\infty)$: its long-observation limit. $P(L)=1/V_{\rm ideal}(L)$: Gaussian precision (inverse coordinate units squared). $\tau$: synaptic decay time (s). $\coth$: hyperbolic cotangent, $\coth z=(e^{2z}+1)/(e^{2z}-1)$; its argument here is dimensionless.
13.paper_location: SI VI, Ideal estimator, S58-S63, PDF p. 13, defines the Gaussian model; S64-S74 on p. 14 gives the covariance solution; S75 on p. 15 displays the finite-$L$ variance and the following paragraph states its limit and characteristic time. Main Eq. 5, PDF p. 4, displays $L^*\le\tau$. The backward precision equation $P'=J-2DP^2$ is the guide's independent reconstruction, not a printed source equation; it confirms S75 despite the sign mismatch in S71.
13.guide_location: [Chapter 6, §6.3, Accounting for diffusion makes readout improve toward a limit](../chapters/ch-memory-readout.html#sec-memory-ideal).
13.status: Paper finite and limiting ideal-readout results, exact within its local Gaussian observation model; guide provides an equivalent precision derivation. The inequality gives a characteristic time, not an abrupt end of benefit.

14.symbols: $T$: storage delay from initial encoding to recall cue (s). $L$: subsequent observation duration (s); source calls it $\Delta T$. $D$: full memory-network diffusion coefficient (coordinate units squared/s). $J$: full-access information rate; $J_{\rm obs}$: observed information rate (both inverse coordinate units squared/s). $0<\alpha\le1$: probability each spike is independently observed, or a verified information fraction; unrelated to coordinate index $\alpha$ in M5. $L^*=1/\sqrt{2DJ}$: full-access characteristic readout time; $L_{\rm obs}^*$: corresponding partial-access time (s). $V_{\rm recall}$: total recall-error variance about the original value. $V_{\rm readout}$: error variance in reading the cue-time state. $V_{\rm ideal,obs}(\infty)$: ideal partial-access limiting readout variance. All $V$ quantities have coordinate units squared. $\tau$: synaptic time (s). The last displayed lower bound uses full access, $\alpha=1$.
14.paper_location: SI VI, S57, PDF p. 12, gives storage-plus-readout error addition. The Incomplete readout paragraph, S82 and Fig. S2, PDF p. 16, replace $J$ by $\alpha J$ and give the time/variance factors. The source's S83 on p. 16 and main Eq. 6 on p. 4 print a stronger lower bound whose direction does not follow. The row's full-access $2DT+\sqrt{2D/J}$ lower limit is guide algebra from S57 and S75, not a displayed corrected source equation. [Error addition](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=12); [finite ideal variance](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=15).
14.guide_location: [Chapter 6, §6.1, Storage loss and readout error add under specific assumptions](../chapters/ch-memory-readout.html#sec-memory-readout-setup); [§6.4, Limited access can make observation slower](../chapters/ch-memory-readout.html#sec-memory-partial); [§6.6, Readout saturates, and one printed error bound needs qualification](../chapters/ch-memory-readout.html#sec-memory-fig3-and-caution).
14.status: Paper error decomposition and partial-access relationships, plus guide derivation of the full-access total-error bound. Error addition needs local unbiasedness and independent future noise. $2D(T+\tau)$ is this asymptotic expression only when the information-diffusion bound is attained, not a general lower bound.

15.symbols: $i$: neuron index. $r_i(t)$: time-dependent firing rate (spikes/s); $\dot r_i$: its time derivative (spikes/s$^2$). $g_i$: total synaptic input in model input units. $\phi(g_i)$: target firing rate at that input (spikes/s). $\tau$: synaptic activation decay time (s). $\tau_m$: firing-rate response time (s), distinct from $\tau$. $D$: scalar diffusion coefficient (coordinate units squared/s). $J$: scalar information rate for that coordinate (inverse coordinate units squared/s).
15.paper_location: SI VII, More than one time constant, S84, PDF p. 17, displays the rate equation; S85-S90 on pp. 17-18 develops the linear modes; S91-S92 on p. 18 display diffusion and its bound. Source S85 prints a positive rate-decay block, although differentiating S84 gives the negative block used in the guide. [Rate model](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=17).
15.guide_location: [Chapter 6, §6.5, Time scales and noise laws change the bound and its equality condition, two-time-constant derivation](../chapters/ch-memory-readout.html#sec-memory-extensions).
15.status: Paper two-stage extension for symmetric weights; the displayed bound is S92 divided by two. The guide repairs the sign of the intermediate linear rate-decay block from the source's own rate equation.

16.symbols: $i$: neuron index. $\theta$: represented scalar coordinate. $\bar r_i$: steady rate (spikes/s); $\bar r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta$: rate slope per coordinate unit. $q_n>0$: common additive Gaussian noise intensity, activation units squared/s; because one spike adds dimensionless activation, its units here are s$^{-1}$. In an activation equation, a noise increment has variance $q_n\,dt$; a rate observation averaged over duration $h$ has noise variance $q_n/h$ (s$^{-2}$). $h$: observation duration (s). $v_i$: retained coordinate shift per activation unit. $D$: scalar diffusion coefficient (coordinate units squared/s). $J$: scalar Gaussian-observation information rate (inverse coordinate units squared/s). $\tau$: synaptic decay time (s). The symbol $q$ mentioned for comparison is the dimensionless place-field threshold, not this noise intensity.
16.paper_location: SI VII, White Gaussian noise, S93-S95, PDF p. 19, changes the noise law and states that a linear transfer rule attains equality. The row's explicit $q_n$ normalization and the matched formulas for $J$ and $D$ are guide reconstructions, not equations printed in that exact form: the supplied S94-S95 omit noise/time factors. The guide chapter writes this noise strength as $q$; the table renames it $q_n$ to avoid the spatial-threshold alias.
16.guide_location: [Chapter 6, §6.5, Time scales and noise laws change the bound and its equality condition, Gaussian-noise reconstruction](../chapters/ch-memory-readout.html#sec-memory-extensions).
16.status: Guide-derived matched Gaussian-noise formulas explaining the paper extension while keeping units explicit. The information-diffusion inequality follows by the same normalized projection proof; symmetric linear transfer is a sufficient equality class.
